entries.name: Successive Halving
entries.definition: A staged best-candidate selection algorithm that divides a resource budget across elimination rounds, evaluates surviving candidates with comparable within-round effort, removes approximately the poorer-performing half, and allocates more effort per remaining candidate in later rounds.
entries.identity_notes: This record retains the common staged-halving algorithm with explicitly separated stochastic and non-stochastic realizations. Jamieson and Talwalkar identify their Successive Halving as the algorithm of Karnin et al., whose source calls it Sequential Halving. That attribution supports a shared identity, not equality of every printed rounding or score formula. One fixed-cohort halving run differs from Hyperband’s bracket hedge, ASHA’s growing asynchronous cohort, BOHB’s learned proposals and PBT’s cross-model weight inheritance. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 259 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 26 lines in each checkout. These were prior candidate leads, source references and neighboring-method mentions, not existing records for these identities. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The 2016 Figure 3 prints a floor-half threshold and a fixed ceil(log2(n)) round count. Literal application to non-power-of-two counts can reach an empty set; ties at its non-strict threshold can retain more than half. The 2013 cardinality rule uses a ceiling instead. These are source conventions requiring explicit implementation choices, not silently equivalent formulas or an author-issued erratum.

The non-stochastic guarantees assume convergent, action-independent loss sequences and sufficient problem-dependent budget. Unknown convergence envelopes prevent a finite observed ranking alone from certifying the eventual best candidate. No universal speedup or finite-budget optimum is asserted.

The budget, cohort and evaluation statistic must be specified. The paper’s doubling construction can remove a prespecified horizon, but does not eliminate all modeling or resource choices. The 2016 PDF footer says volume 41; bibliographic metadata follows the publisher’s volume 51.

claims.statement: Start with a finite candidate set and a total allocation budget, divide effort across elimination rounds, evaluate the current survivors, retain their better-performing subset, and repeat with fewer candidates and more effort per survivor. The original stochastic Sequential Halving allocates floor(T/(|S|*ceil(log2(n)))) samples per surviving arm in a round, ranks stage empirical reward averages, and keeps ceil(|S|/2) arms with the highest averages. The non-stochastic hyperparameter formulation instead allocates additional training pulls and compares current validation losses at cumulative training progress; it minimizes these losses rather than averaging raw observations as if they were i.i.d. rewards. Its analysis assumes fixed loss sequences with limits but does not require the convergence envelopes as inputs. Randomly sampled or prespecified configurations can supply the finite cohort. Resume within a candidate’s own training trajectory; the mechanism does not copy weights between candidates.

entries.name: Asynchronous Successive Halving
entries.definition: An asynchronous resource-allocation algorithm that promotes promising completed hyperparameter trials through increasing resource levels as workers become available and starts new trials when no eligible promotion is available, without waiting for an entire evaluation stage to finish.
entries.identity_notes: ASHA is the asynchronous promotion procedure, not every early-stopping scheduler, the complete distributed training system, or a synonym for Hyperband or BOHB. A rung contains evaluations at one resource level; a bracket sets the starting resource and rung schedule. Multiple ASHA brackets can implement asynchronous Hyperband, while a single ASHA bracket does not include that wrapper. The source’s bounded promotion variant is the primary scope here. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 259 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 26 lines in each checkout. These were prior candidate leads, source references and neighboring-method mentions, not existing records for these identities. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The MLSys PDF’s Algorithm 2 places the new-trial fallback inside its descending-rung loop. The author’s dissertation Algorithm 3 places it after that loop, consistent with the method prose. The record follows the latter and retains the discrepancy; it does not claim byte-equivalent pseudocode or an author-issued erratum.

The top-fraction notation does not specify every discrete rounding, tie or failed-job policy. The literal schedule reaches r*eta^floor(log_eta(R/r)), which equals R only when the ratio aligns with a power of eta; implementations must define any terminal-budget adjustment.

Early rankings and completion order can affect promotions. The paper’s discussion of vanishing mispromotions is not imported as an unconditional theorem for dependent upper-rung observations. No universal parallel speedup or finite-budget optimum is asserted.
Only the declared methods and dissertation pages were inspected. System-specific scheduling, autoscaling, benchmark results and executable implementations are outside this record’s claims.

claims.statement: Choose minimum and maximum resources r and R, a reduction factor eta, and starting-level offset s. Resource at rung k is r*eta^(s+k). Dispatch work to free workers and record completed rung losses. In the author dissertation’s Algorithm 3, scan promotable rungs from the highest eligible level downward, stopping below the maximum-resource rung. At each level, consider the currently best approximately 1/eta fraction of completed configurations and select an eligible one that has not already been promoted. If the entire scan yields none, sample a new configuration for the base rung. Thus the starting cohort can grow and promotions do not wait for every job at a rung. Promoted configurations may later fall outside the hindsight top fraction as additional results arrive. Checkpointing can reuse a trial’s previous training; it is distinct from copying weights between different configurations. The maximum resource limits promotion depth in this bounded version.

entries.definition: A hyperparameter optimization procedure that evaluates a finite Cartesian product of chosen values for each configuration variable and selects a configuration using its validation performance.

native_neighbors.name: Hyperband
native_neighbors.definition: A hyperparameter resource-allocation algorithm that runs successive-halving brackets with different initial configuration counts and starting budgets, balancing broad early screening against more conservative evaluation.

claims.statement: Choose a maximum per-configuration resource R and reduction factor eta. In the finite-horizon Algorithm1, set s_max=floor(log_eta(R)) and B=(s_max+1)*R. For each bracket s from s_max down to zero, start with n=ceil((B/R)*eta^s/(s+1)) configurations and r=R*eta^(−s) resource units. Evaluate current candidates at geometrically increasing resource levels and retain the best approximately 1/eta fraction after each comparison. The s=0 bracket evaluates its candidates directly at R. Algorithm1 returns the configuration with the smallest intermediate loss observed, rather than specifying selection only among maximum-budget evaluations. Brackets address uncertainty about how many configurations to start and how long to evaluate before elimination. Resources can denote iterations, time, data or features; actual computational cost and whether work can be resumed depend on that choice.

evidence.locator: Sections3.1–3.6, PDF/printed pp.6–12; Algorithm1 on p.8 and Table1 on p.9; sampling generalization in Section2.1 on p.5

The pinned AIO target describes training strategies as preprocessing; the relation connects these scopes without asserting that this search algorithm is preprocessing, an identical concept, or a subclass.

native_neighbors.name: BOHB

claims.statement: Keep observations separated by evaluation budget. For proposals, use the highest budget with enough data to build better- and worse-performing configuration densities. The paper uses multivariate KDEs, a loss-quantile split with minimum set sizes, and finite candidate sampling from an expanded better-performing density, selecting a candidate with favorable l(x)/g(x). Retain a positive fraction of random configurations, and fall back to random sampling when no model is available. Hyperband brackets and successive halving then allocate increasing resources to surviving candidates. Observations are shared across brackets, but the proposal density is not fitted by pooling all fidelity levels indiscriminately. The method can schedule multiple brackets and concurrent evaluations; the paper’s worker policy favors waiting smaller-budget jobs. native_neighbors.name: Tree-structured Parzen Estimator
native_neighbors.definition: A sequential hyperparameter optimization method that separates observations by a loss quantile, fits tree-structured densities for the better and remaining configurations, and proposes evaluations using their density ratio as an expected-improvement ranking.

claims.statement: Represent valid configurations with a conditional generative tree so that some variables are active only for particular parent choices. Given observed configurations and losses to minimize, choose a loss threshold at a quantile gamma and fit l(x) from observations below that threshold and g(x) from the remainder. The model uses p(x|y)=l(x) below the threshold and g(x) otherwise, with p(x)=gamma*l(x)+(1−gamma)*g(x). Under this construction, expected nonnegative improvement E[max(y*−y,0)] is proportional, across configurations, to [gamma+(1−gamma)*g(x)/l(x)]^−1 wherever the relevant densities and expectation are defined. Draw candidate configurations from l, rank them by this expression, evaluate the selected candidate’s actual loss, and incorporate the observation into subsequent density estimates. The original estimator replaces continuous priors with adaptive Parzen mixtures around observed values and retains a prior component; bounded uniform variables use truncated Gaussian mixtures, log-uniform variables are modeled in log space, and categorical probabilities are reweighted by observed counts. The tree specifies conditional variable activation, not a decision tree that predicts loss. This is distinct from the separate Gaussian-process surrogate described in Section 3 of the same paper.

evidence.locator: Section 1 conditional configuration spaces, Section 2 and Equation (1), and Sections 4–4.2 with Equations (2)–(3), PDF pp. 2–4

limitations: The ratio ranking assumes the paper’s two-region conditional model and a finite, positive improvement constant. It is not the numerical value of expected improvement without that constant, nor an optimality or calibration guarantee.

The derivation after Equation (3) prints an integral without the factor y in an expanded numerator. The unexpanded integral of (y*−y)*p(y) gives the density-ratio ranking recorded here. The original tree-structured factorization encodes conditional activation and the specified density families. It does not establish arbitrary dependency modeling or identity with later multivariate TPE variants.

native_neighbors.name: Population Based Training
native_neighbors.definition: A population-based neural-network training procedure that interleaves parameter updates with performance-guided copying of partially trained models and exploration of hyperparameters, producing training trajectories with changing hyperparameter settings.

claims.statement: Maintain population members with model parameters, hyperparameters, an evaluation score and training progress. Each worker trains its parameters with its current hyperparameters and evaluates a chosen performance metric, which need not be differentiable or identical to the local training objective. When a readiness condition holds, an exploitation rule can replace that worker’s parameters and hyperparameters with those of another promising member. An exploration rule then perturbs or resamples the copied hyperparameters, and training continues from the inherited weights. Algorithm 1 calls exploration and re-evaluation only when exploitation changes the weights; its final output is the population member’s parameters with the highest recorded score. Readiness, selection and mutation rules depend on the application. The original procedure is asynchronous: members need access to population scores, parameters and hyperparameters, but no population-wide synchronization barrier is required. Alternating local parameter learning with slower model selection and hyperparameter changes yields schedules along training lineages, rather than restricting each run to one fixed hyperparameter configuration.

evidence.locator: Section 3, Equations (1)–(4) and Algorithm 1, PDF pp. 4–6; identity and related work on pp. 1–4

limitations: The original algorithm specifies application-dependent readiness, exploitation and exploration. PBA’s quartile selection, three-epoch interval, operation probabilities and schedule-only transfer are not general PBT requirements.
Asynchrony removes a global training barrier but does not remove the need to exchange model state and performance information. Reusing weights is not weight averaging or an inference-time ensemble.
